title: Les allergies croisées aux pollens et à certains fruits augmentent - Radio France
summary: Radio France reports a rise in cross-reactive allergies between pollens and certain fruits, often presenting as oral allergy syndrome. Experts point to increased pollen exposure and allergen similarity as drivers. content:
Radio France and medical practitioners are reporting an increase in cross-reactive allergies connecting common pollens and certain fruits. Many patients experience oral allergy symptoms during pollen season, a pattern that specialists link to immune sensitization to pollen proteins that resemble proteins found in fresh fruits and some vegetables.

This phenomenon, often called pollen-food syndrome or oral allergy syndrome, occurs when antibodies formed against pollens react to similar proteins in foods. Common examples noted by allergists include birch pollen cross-reacting with apple, pear, hazelnut or carrot proteins, and ragweed sensitivities that can be associated with reactions to melon or banana. The severity ranges from mild oral itching and swelling to, in rarer cases, more systemic reactions.

Physicians point to several likely contributing factors. Longer and more intense pollen seasons, higher pollen concentrations, and broader exposure in urban and suburban areas appear to increase the number of people who develop pollen sensitization. Changes in environmental conditions and shifting plant distribution are also cited as elements that may influence exposure patterns.

Symptoms typically include itching or tingling in the mouth and throat shortly after eating the trigger food, mild swelling of lips or tongue, and occasionally gastrointestinal discomfort. While many cases remain limited to oral symptoms, clinicians warn that more significant allergic reactions can occur, especially when multiple allergens are involved or when the patient has a history of severe allergies.

Health professionals recommend that individuals who suspect cross-reactive allergies consult an allergist for evaluation. Diagnostic options include skin prick testing and blood tests for specific IgE antibodies. Identifying the exact triggers helps patients manage risks and adjust diets safely.

Practical advice for affected people includes avoiding raw forms of the implicated fruits and vegetables, since cooking often denatures the proteins responsible for cross-reactivity and reduces the chance of a reaction. Those with a history of severe reactions should carry emergency medication, including an epinephrine auto-injector when prescribed. For longer-term relief, allergists may discuss targeted therapies such as pollen immunotherapy, which can reduce overall pollen sensitivity and sometimes lessen associated food reactions.

Public health bodies and pollen forecasting services continue to monitor trends and advise susceptible populations during peak seasons. Radio France reports that clinics are seeing more consultations focused specifically on pollen-related food reactions, and specialists urge awareness, timely testing, and personalized management plans.

As the situation evolves, physicians emphasize prevention and education: understanding personal triggers, following pollen forecasts when possible, and seeking professional guidance to reduce the risk of severe outcomes. Radio France will continue following updates from allergists and health authorities on this growing concern.

## What is pollen-food syndrome

This phenomenon, often called pollen-food syndrome or oral allergy syndrome, occurs when antibodies formed against pollens react to similar proteins in foods. The severity ranges from mild oral itching and swelling to, in rarer cases, more systemic reactions.

## Common cross-reactions

- Birch pollen can cross-react with apple, pear, hazelnut or carrot proteins.
- Ragweed sensitivities can be associated with reactions to melon or banana.

## Contributing factors

Physicians point to several likely contributing factors:

- Longer and more intense pollen seasons.
- Higher pollen concentrations.
- Broader exposure in urban and suburban areas.
- Changes in environmental conditions and shifting plant distribution affecting exposure patterns.

## Symptoms

Symptoms typically include:

- Itching or tingling in the mouth and throat shortly after eating the trigger food.
- Mild swelling of lips or tongue.
- Occasionally gastrointestinal discomfort.

While many cases remain limited to oral symptoms, clinicians warn that more significant allergic reactions can occur, especially when multiple allergens are involved or when the patient has a history of severe allergies.

## Diagnosis and testing

Health professionals recommend that individuals who suspect cross-reactive allergies consult an allergist for evaluation. Diagnostic options include:

- Skin prick testing.
- Blood tests for specific IgE antibodies.

Identifying the exact triggers helps patients manage risks and adjust diets safely.

## Management and prevention

Practical advice for affected people includes:

- Avoiding raw forms of the implicated fruits and vegetables, since cooking often denatures the proteins responsible for cross-reactivity and reduces the chance of a reaction.
- Carrying emergency medication, including an epinephrine auto-injector when prescribed, for those with a history of severe reactions.
- Discussing longer-term options such as pollen immunotherapy with an allergist, which can reduce overall pollen sensitivity and sometimes lessen associated food reactions.

Public health bodies and pollen forecasting services continue to monitor trends and advise susceptible populations during peak seasons.
